container.short: The box your video is stored in.
container.eli5: Think of it as the box, not the toy. The box doesn't change how good your video looks. It decides which apps can open the file and what happens if your PC crashes while recording.

mp4.short: The format almost everything can play.
mp4.eli5: The most common video box in the world. Phones, Discord, YouTube and every video editor understand it.
pros: Starts playing sooner when streamed from the web
cons: If your PC crashes or loses power mid-recording, the file can be lost
mp4.pickIf: You make short recordings and share them straight away. Replay clips are a regular MP4 either way.

mp4-fragmented.eli5: A normal MP4 writes its table of contents at the very end, so a crash means no table of contents and a broken file. Crash-safe MP4 writes small self-contained chunks as it goes, so a crash only loses the last second or two.
pros: A crash won't ruin a long recording
Replay clips save as a regular MP4
cons: A few older editors seek through it a little slower
mp4-fragmented.pickIf: You record long sessions and want MP4 without the risk. This is a great default.

mkv.eli5: A very flexible box that accepts any video or audio type and lots of separate audio tracks. If your PC crashes, everything recorded up to that moment is still playable.
pros: Holds any codec and many audio tracks
cons: Some phones, social sites and older editors won't accept it
mkv.pickIf: You edit before you share. Turn on "Convert to MP4 when done" to get the best of both.

mov.short: Apple's video format, loved by editors.
mov.eli5: Apple's version of the video box. Final Cut and DaVinci Resolve like it, especially with uncompressed audio.
cons: Not crash-safe
Files get large with uncompressed audio
mov.pickIf: You edit in DaVinci Resolve or on a Mac.

mov-fragmented.eli5: The same chunk-by-chunk trick as crash-safe MP4, applied to MOV.
pros: Replay clips save as a regular MOV
cons: Some players handle long recordings a little worse than regular MOV

mpegts.short: A format built for live TV.
mpegts.eli5: Designed for broadcast, where the signal can drop at any time. Every piece of the file stands on its own, so it never really breaks.
cons: Slightly larger files
Not every editor imports it smoothly
mpegts.pickIf: A specific tool or workflow asks for it.

webm.eli5: A box made for web browsers. It only holds AV1 video and Opus audio here, which keeps files small and plays right inside Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
cons: Only works with AV1 video and Opus audio
Many editors don't like it

flv.eli5: A leftover from the Flash days. It's only here for old tools that still expect it.
cons: Outdated
Only H.264 video and AAC audio
Not crash-safe
flv.pickIf: Only if an old tool requires it.

remux.short: Rewraps an MKV into an MP4 after you stop.
remux.eli5: Record into the crash-safe MKV box, then move the video into an MP4 box when you're done. Nothing is re-compressed, so it takes seconds and loses zero quality.
pros: Crash safety while recording, easy sharing afterwards
cons: Briefly uses extra disk space while converting

h264.eli5: The most compatible codec there is. Anything made in the last 15 years can play it.
cons: Biggest files of the three for the same quality
No HDR
h264.pickIf: You never want to think about compatibility.

hevc.short: Smaller files than H.264, same quality.
hevc.eli5: The successor to H.264. It squeezes the same picture into roughly a third less space and supports HDR.
cons: Some browsers and Discord previews struggle with it
Windows may need the free HEVC extension to play it
hevc.pickIf: You keep lots of footage or record HDR games.

av1.eli5: A modern, royalty-free codec backed by YouTube, Netflix and friends. It makes the smallest files of the three at the same quality.
cons: Hardware AV1 needs a newer GPU (RTX 40+, Intel Arc, Radeon RX 7000+)
Older devices can't play it

encoder.short: The worker that compresses your video.
encoder.eli5: Hardware encoders are tiny dedicated chips on your graphics card, separate from the part that runs your game, so they barely cost any FPS. Software encoders run on your CPU: they can look great, but they can steal performance from your game.
encoder.pickIf: Pick a hardware encoder (NVIDIA, AMD or Intel) unless you have a strong reason not to.

nvenc-h264.short: NVIDIA's built-in encoder, in the most compatible format.
nvenc-h264.eli5: Your GeForce card has a separate chip just for video. It records while your game keeps the rest of the GPU. This is what ShadowPlay uses.
cons: NVIDIA GPUs only
Bigger files than HEVC or AV1
nvenc-h264.pickIf: You have an NVIDIA card and want maximum compatibility.

nvenc-hevc.eli5: The same dedicated NVIDIA video chip, speaking the more efficient HEVC language.
cons: NVIDIA GPUs only
Slightly less compatible than H.264
nvenc-hevc.pickIf: You have an NVIDIA card and want better quality per megabyte.

nvenc-av1.eli5: The newest NVIDIA video chips can speak AV1, the most efficient codec available.
cons: Needs an RTX 40-series card or newer
Older devices can't play AV1
nvenc-av1.pickIf: You have an RTX 40-series or newer card.

amf-h264.short: AMD's built-in encoder, most compatible format.
amf-h264.eli5: Radeon cards have their own dedicated video chip too. This uses it to make H.264 files.
pros: Almost no FPS cost on AMD
cons: AMD GPUs only
H.264 quality trails NVIDIA a little at low bitrates
amf-h264.pickIf: You have an AMD card and want compatibility.

amf-hevc.eli5: AMD's video chip, speaking HEVC. This is where AMD's encoder really shines.
pros: Almost no FPS cost on AMD
cons: AMD GPUs only
amf-hevc.pickIf: You have an AMD card. This is usually the best AMD choice.

amf-av1.eli5: Newer Radeon cards can encode AV1 in hardware.
cons: Needs a Radeon RX 7000-series card or newer

qsv-h264.short: Intel's built-in encoder, most compatible format.
qsv-h264.eli5: Most Intel CPUs have built-in graphics with a video chip called Quick Sync. Using it leaves your main graphics card completely free for the game.
pros: Free if your CPU has it
Doesn't touch your gaming GPU at all
cons: Quality trails NVENC a little on older chips
qsv-h264.pickIf: You have an Intel CPU with graphics and want your GPU 100% on the game.

cons: Intel graphics only

qsv-av1.eli5: Intel Arc cards and newer Intel CPUs can make AV1 files in hardware.
cons: Needs Intel Arc or a recent Intel Core Ultra CPU

x264.eli5: Runs on your processor instead of a video chip. At slow settings it squeezes out excellent quality, but it works your CPU hard and can lower your FPS.
cons: Heavy CPU use
Can cause stutter in CPU-hungry games
x264.pickIf: You have lots of spare CPU cores or no hardware encoder.

x265.eli5: The CPU version of HEVC. Very efficient files, but very demanding.
cons: Very heavy CPU use: often too slow for live gameplay
x265.pickIf: Rarely, for live recording. Prefer a hardware HEVC encoder.

svt-av1.eli5: A software AV1 encoder built by Intel and Netflix to be quick. Still a lot of CPU work, but usable on strong processors.
cons: Heavy CPU use
svt-av1.pickIf: You want AV1, your GPU can't do it, and you have a strong CPU.

aom-av1.short: The reference AV1 encoder. Very slow.
aom-av1.eli5: The original AV1 encoder. Great quality, but far too slow for most live recording.
cons: Extremely slow
Will likely hurt game performance
aom-av1.pickIf: Almost never for live capture. Use SVT-AV1 or a hardware encoder instead.

rate-control.short: How the encoder decides how much data to spend.
rate-control.eli5: Every second of video gets a data budget. Rate control is the rule for spending it: the same amount every second, more on busy moments, or whatever a chosen quality level needs.

cbr.short: The same amount of data every second.
cbr.eli5: Like a tap stuck on one setting: a steady flow no matter what's on screen.
cons: Wastes space on calm scenes
Can get blurry in chaotic scenes
cbr.pickIf: You need a predictable file size.

vbr.short: More data for action, less for menus.
vbr.eli5: Spends extra data on explosions and fast camera turns, and saves it during calm moments. Same average size, better-looking video.
pros: Better quality for the same average size
cons: Final file size is less predictable
vbr.pickIf: You record to disk. A great default.

cqp.short: Pick a quality; the file is as big as it needs to be.
cqp.eli5: Instead of a data budget, you pick how good it should look and the encoder spends whatever it takes. Calm scenes stay tiny, intense scenes get big.
cons: Unpredictable size: fast action can make huge files
cqp.pickIf: You record locally and have plenty of disk space.

bitrate.short: How much data each second of video gets.
bitrate.eli5: More megabits per second means a sharper picture and bigger files. A good starting point for 1080p at 60 FPS is 15–25 Mbps for H.264; HEVC and AV1 look just as good with about 30% less.
pros: Higher = sharper, especially in fast motion
cons: Higher = bigger files and more RAM for Instant Replay

max-bitrate.eli5: With variable bitrate, this is the most data any single second is allowed to use. It stops sudden spikes from making the file huge.

quality-level.short: Lower number = better quality, bigger file.
quality-level.eli5: A quality dial where smaller numbers look better. Around 18–23 looks great for gameplay; below 16 is usually wasted space.
cons: Each step down makes files noticeably bigger

keyframe-interval.short: How often a complete picture is saved.
keyframe-interval.eli5: Most frames only store what changed since the last one. A keyframe is a full picture. More frequent keyframes make clips start exactly where you want and make scrubbing smoother; less frequent ones save a little space. 0 lets Backsight choose (2 seconds).
pros: 1–2 seconds: precise Instant Replay cuts, easy editing
cons: Very short intervals waste space

preset.eli5: Slower presets make the encoder think harder about every frame: better quality at the same file size, but more work. For hardware encoders that work happens on the video chip, so it rarely costs FPS until the slowest settings at high resolutions.

tuning.short: What the encoder should optimize for.
tuning.eli5: Tells the encoder what matters most: the best picture, the lowest delay (for streaming and remote play), or perfect, uncompressed-looking quality.

tune-hq.short: Best picture. The right choice for recording.
tune-hq.eli5: Spends a little extra time per frame for a better image. Recording doesn't care about a few milliseconds of delay, so this is what you want.
tune-hq.pickIf: You're recording or using Instant Replay.

tune-uhq.short: Even better picture, more GPU work.
tune-uhq.eli5: Squeezes out extra quality for HEVC and AV1 on newer NVIDIA cards at the cost of more encoder work.
cons: HEVC/AV1 and newer GPUs only
Uses more GPU memory

tune-ll.eli5: Gets each frame out the door faster. Matters for live streaming and remote play, not for recording.

tune-ull.eli5: Fastest possible output for things like game streaming to another device.

tune-lossless.eli5: Keeps every single pixel exactly as it was. Files can be tens of gigabytes per hour.
cons: Enormous files
Not suitable for Instant Replay

multipass.short: The encoder looks at each frame twice.
multipass.eli5: A quick first look helps the encoder decide where to spend data before doing the real work. A quarter-resolution first look is cheap and helps; a full-resolution one helps more but costs more GPU.

multipass-off.short: One look per frame. Fastest and lightest.
multipass-off.eli5: The encoder compresses each frame in a single go.

multipass-quarter.short: A cheap first look. Cleaner fast motion.
multipass-quarter.eli5: The first look is at a small version of the frame, so it's quick but still helps quality, especially in fast motion.

multipass-full.short: A detailed first look. Best quality, most work.
multipass-full.eli5: The first look is at the full frame. Slightly better quality, but noticeably more encoder work at 1440p and 4K.

profile.short: Which feature set the video uses.
profile.eli5: A promise about which compression tricks are used, so players know whether they can play it. For H.264, High is the best and universally supported. For HEVC, Main 10 is needed for 10-bit and HDR.

lookahead.short: The encoder peeks at upcoming frames.
lookahead.eli5: By looking a few frames into the future, the encoder can see a big change coming and plan its data budget. Helps fast action look cleaner.
cons: Uses noticeably more memory and some GPU work

spatial-aq.short: Extra detail where blockiness shows the most.
spatial-aq.eli5: Flat areas like skies, fog and dark corners show ugly blocks first. This spends a bit more data there so they stay smooth.
pros: Fewer visible blocks in skies and dark scenes
cons: Fine textures may get slightly less data
Some extra GPU work while you play

temporal-aq.short: Extra detail for things that stay still.
temporal-aq.eli5: Parts of the screen that don't move, like your HUD, get a little extra quality since they're seen for a long time.

b-frames.short: Frames that borrow from before and after.
b-frames.eli5: Some frames can be built from the frames before and after them, which saves space. They make the encoder work a little harder; on NVIDIA cards Backsight uses 0 to stay light.
pros: Smaller files at the same quality
cons: A little more work for the encoder
Tiny bit of delay (irrelevant for recording)

encoder-usage.short: What AMD's encoder should be tuned for.
encoder-usage.eli5: AMD's version of tuning: recording and transcoding favor quality, low latency favors speed.

row-mt.short: Lets the encoder use more CPU cores.
row-mt.eli5: Splits each frame into rows so more CPU cores can work at once. Faster, with almost no quality cost.

resolution.short: How big the saved video is.
resolution.eli5: "Same as source" keeps every pixel. Scaling down (say, 1440p to 1080p) saves space and encoder work, and still looks good on phones and Discord.

frame-rate.eli5: 60 FPS looks smooth for games. 30 FPS halves the work and files feel choppier. 120 FPS and above is great for slow-motion edits but needs more bitrate.
cons: Higher = more data and encoder work

resolution-source.eli5: Nothing is scaled down. Best for reading small text, but your PC encodes the most pixels.

resolution-2160p.short: Ultra sharp, never bigger than your screen.
resolution-2160p.eli5: 2160 pixels tall on a normal widescreen. On a smaller screen it just keeps your screen's size.

resolution-1440p.short: Sharp, never bigger than your screen.
resolution-1440p.eli5: 1440 pixels tall on a normal widescreen. A middle ground between 1080p and 4K.

resolution-1080p.short: Sharp, light, and easy to share.
resolution-1080p.eli5: 1080 pixels tall on a normal widescreen. Looks good on phones and Discord and is light on your PC.

resolution-720p.eli5: 720 pixels tall on a normal widescreen. Very light on your PC, but text looks fuzzier.

fps-30.eli5: 30 pictures every second. Your PC does half the work of 60 FPS, but fast games look choppier.

fps-60.eli5: 60 pictures every second. Motion looks fluid without asking too much from your PC.

fps-120.eli5: 120 pictures every second. Good for slow-motion edits, but raise Bitrate so each picture stays sharp.

fps-144.eli5: 144 pictures every second, the speed of many gaming monitors. The most encoder work; raise Bitrate to keep it sharp.

capture-cursor.eli5: Turn it off for games where the pointer is hidden anyway, or for clean screenshots.

file-splitting.short: Start a new file every so often.
file-splitting.eli5: Long recordings are saved as several smaller files instead of one giant one. Easier to move, upload and edit. 0 turns it off.

instant-replay.eli5: Backsight quietly keeps the last few minutes in memory. When something cool happens, press your hotkey and those minutes are saved as a clip. Nothing is written to your drive until you save.
pros: No huge recordings to clean up
cons: Uses some RAM while it's on

clip-shape.short: Wide like your screen, tall for phones, or both.
clip-shape.eli5: Sites like YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Reels want tall clips. Vertical cuts the middle of the picture into a tall clip after you save; it takes a little while in the background and never slows the save. Recordings always stay wide.

clip-shape-wide.short: Clips look exactly like your screen.
clip-shape-wide.eli5: Nothing extra happens after a save. Best for YouTube, Discord and watching on a PC.

clip-shape-vertical.short: Each clip becomes a tall clip of the middle of your screen.
clip-shape-vertical.eli5: Backsight saves the clip, then turns it into a tall one named '(vertical)'. The sides of the picture are cut off. If that fails, you keep the wide clip.

clip-shape-both.short: Keep the wide clip and also get a tall one.
clip-shape-both.eli5: You get two files: the normal clip and a '(vertical)' copy of its middle. Uses a bit more disk space.

replay-length.short: How far back a saved clip goes.
replay-length.eli5: Longer replays need more memory. The estimate below the slider shows how much RAM your current settings will use.

audio-encoder.eli5: Like video, audio can be compressed (small files, tiny quality loss) or kept perfect (bigger files).

aac.eli5: The standard sound format for MP4 videos. Sounds great at 160 kbps and above.
cons: Slight quality loss (inaudible at normal bitrates)
aac.pickIf: You want it to just work. The best default.

opus.short: Better sound per kilobyte than AAC.
opus.eli5: A modern audio format, used by Discord and YouTube. Sounds better than AAC at the same size.
cons: Some editors and older devices don't support it

flac.eli5: Lossless: you get back exactly what was recorded, just packed tighter. About half the size of uncompressed audio.
cons: Larger than AAC/Opus
Some players skip it inside MP4

alac.eli5: Apple's lossless format. Same idea as FLAC, but friendlier for Apple apps.
cons: Larger than AAC/Opus

pcm-16.eli5: Raw audio with no compression at all. Editors love it. About 11 MB per minute for stereo.
cons: Large files
MKV and MOV only

pcm-24.eli5: Raw audio with more headroom than CD quality. About 17 MB per minute for stereo.
pros: Perfect quality with headroom for editing
cons: Large files
MKV and MOV only

pcm-32f.eli5: Raw audio that can't distort from being too loud, even if levels go over the top. About 23 MB per minute for stereo.
cons: Largest files
MKV and MOV only

audio-bitrate.short: How much data each second of sound gets.
audio-bitrate.eli5: 160 kbps sounds great for gameplay. 320 kbps is near-perfect. Audio is tiny compared to video, so there's little reason to go low.

compression-level.short: How hard to pack lossless audio.
compression-level.eli5: Higher numbers make slightly smaller files and use slightly more CPU. Quality is always perfect either way.

desktop-audio.eli5: Game sounds, music, Discord voices: whatever comes out of your speakers or headset.

microphone.eli5: Records your mic alongside the game. Use the mute or push-to-talk hotkeys to control it while you play.

app-audio.eli5: Focus the game on your primary monitor when starting capture. Backsight keeps recording that game's sound when you switch windows. Restart capture to choose another game.
pros: No music or chat in your clips
cons: Needs Windows 10 version 2004 or newer

audio-tracks.short: Keep each audio source on its own track.
audio-tracks.eli5: The first track contains all your sound for normal playback. Each enabled source also gets its own track, so you can adjust it later in an editor.
cons: Most players and sites only play the first track
MKV and MOV handle this best

captions.short: Write out what you say in each clip.
captions.eli5: After a clip is saved, Backsight listens to it right here on your PC and writes your words into a .srt file next to the clip; nothing is sent anywhere. Video players like VLC and sites like YouTube show that file as subtitles. Vertical clips get the words written right into the picture, ready for TikTok and Shorts.
pros: Viewers can follow with the sound off
Works offline after a one-time download of about 61 MB
cons: Turn on Separate audio tracks, or voices in the game may be written out too
Takes a little while after each save

screenshot-format.eli5: PNG keeps every pixel perfect, JPEG and WebP make much smaller files with a tiny bit of loss, and JPEG XR keeps HDR brightness.

png.eli5: Lossless, so text and UI stay razor sharp. Files are a few megabytes each.
cons: Bigger files
png.pickIf: You want the best quality. A great default.

jpeg.eli5: Compresses the image so it's a fraction of PNG's size. At quality 90 you'll struggle to spot the difference.
cons: Slight blur around sharp text at low quality

webp.short: Smaller than JPEG at the same quality.
webp.eli5: A modern web image format. Looks like JPEG at roughly two-thirds of the size.
cons: A few older apps can't open it

jxr.eli5: Normal image formats can't store the extra brightness of HDR, so HDR screenshots look washed out. JPEG XR keeps it. Xbox Game Bar uses the same format.
cons: Limited app support
jxr.pickIf: You play in HDR and want screenshots that look the way the game did.

screenshot-quality.eli5: Only used by JPEG and WebP. 90 is the sweet spot; 100 is close to perfect but much bigger.

copy-to-clipboard.eli5: Each screenshot is also copied, so you can press Ctrl+V right away in a chat or document.

hotkey.short: A key combo that works even in-game.
hotkey.eli5: Press it any time, even while a game is focused. Click a hotkey box, press the combination you want, and it's set. Mouse side buttons work too.

hotkey-conflict.short: Two actions share the same keys.
hotkey-conflict.eli5: Only one of them could fire, so Backsight asks you to change one. Also watch out for combos your games or other apps already use.

overlay.short: Apps that listen for their own keys while you play.
overlay.eli5: Discord, the NVIDIA app, Steam and others have hotkeys too, often for their own clips or an overlay (a panel over your game). When one uses a Backsight key, one press may do two things, or Backsight may not see the key at all. Give Backsight other keys, or change the key in that app.

output-folder.short: Where your clips and screenshots go.
output-folder.eli5: By default Backsight uses Videos\Backsight and Pictures\Backsight. Pick a fast drive with plenty of space for long recordings.

name-after-game.short: Files start with the game's name.
name-after-game.eli5: A clip saved while you play Tomb Raider is called "Tomb Raider 2026-11-12 01.15.07.mp4" instead of "Backsight …". Backsight uses the program you have kept in front for a few seconds. On the desktop, or when a program has no usable name, files still start with "Backsight".

video-hdr.short: Keep bright highlights in clips and recordings.
video-hdr.eli5: Turning this on also picks what HDR needs: NVIDIA NVENC HEVC and an MP4 or MKV file. Turn on HDR in Windows for the monitor your game is on. Whenever HDR can't be recorded, Backsight records standard video and says why on Home.

capture-target.short: The whole monitor, or just the game's window.
capture-target.eli5: Whole monitor records everything you see, pop-ups and other apps included. Game window only records the first program you keep in front for a few seconds, usually your game, and sticks with it until its window closes. Home always says what is happening, for example when the window is minimized or closed.

capture-target-monitor.eli5: What you see is what you get. It works with every game, including exclusive full screen, and needs no setup.

capture-target-window.short: Records just the game, nothing around it.
capture-target-window.eli5: Backsight records the window of the program you keep in front for a few seconds, so start your game first. Switching to a chat or a browser doesn't change what is recorded; only another program filling the whole screen takes over, never a browser. After the game window closes, the next program you keep in front is recorded, so check Home if you're unsure.

capture-monitor.eli5: Pick the monitor your games run on. If that monitor is unplugged, Backsight records your main monitor and says so on Home, then goes back to your pick when it's connected again.

folder-per-game.short: Each game gets its own folder.
folder-per-game.eli5: Clips, recordings and screenshots go in a folder named after the game, such as Videos\Backsight\Tomb Raider. Files saved on the desktop stay in the main folder. The Library still shows everything together.

start-with-windows.short: Be ready the moment you log in.
start-with-windows.eli5: Backsight starts quietly in the system tray, so Instant Replay is already running when you launch a game.

minimize-to-tray.short: Closing the window doesn't stop Backsight.
minimize-to-tray.eli5: The window closes and its memory is freed, but hotkeys and Instant Replay keep working from the tray icon by the clock.

notifications.short: A small card for everything Backsight does.
notifications.eli5: A Backsight card slides in (top right unless you move it) when a recording starts or stops, a clip or screenshot is saved, and so on. It never takes your mouse or keyboard away from the game, and it never shows up in your videos.

sounds.short: A short sound for every action.
sounds.eli5: A different short sound for recording, saving, screenshots and the mic, so you know it worked without looking. It works in every game, even full screen. The sound plays on your speakers, so one made during a recording is in the video too.

recording-indicator.short: A red dot on screen while you record.
recording-indicator.eli5: While a recording runs, a red dot with the time sits on screen (top right unless you move it), with a microphone symbol when push-to-talk is open or the mic is muted. The Backsight icon by the clock turns red too. Like pop-ups, it never shows up in your videos, and games in exclusive full screen hide it.

hud-position.short: Drag the dot and pop-ups anywhere.
hud-position.eli5: Press Move, then drag the sample dot and pop-up wherever you like on your screen. Press Done to keep that spot. Back to corner puts them top right again.

advanced-mode.eli5: Simple mode shows the handful of settings most people need. Advanced reveals everything else. Every setting still has an explanation, so feel free to explore.

updates.short: Gets the newest Backsight from GitHub.
updates.eli5: Backsight checks for a newer version when it starts, every hour, and when you press Check. Install downloads it, checks it's really from Backsight, then closes and reopens Backsight. A recording in progress is saved first.

early-updates.short: Test versions arrive about two days before everyone else.
early-updates.eli5: Each new Backsight goes to early testers first. If nothing goes wrong in about two days, everyone gets it. Turn this off any time; you then get the next version everyone gets.

first-run-setup.short: Checks your PC and picks what records.
first-run-setup.eli5: Backsight tests which encoders work on your PC and picks the one that costs your games the least. It also checks whether NVIDIA's overlay uses the same keys. Run it again after you change graphics cards.

diag-buffer-length.short: How much replay is stored right now.
diag-buffer-length.eli5: This is how far back a saved clip can reach right now. It grows after Instant Replay starts, then stays at the length you chose.

diag-buffer-memory.short: The RAM the stored replay uses.
diag-buffer-memory.eli5: Instant Replay keeps your last few minutes in memory as already-compressed video and audio. This is how much memory that takes, and it never goes past its limit.

diag-buffer-rate.short: Average size of the stored video and audio.
diag-buffer-rate.eli5: This is the stored data divided by the time it covers, so it is a rough average, not an exact bitrate. It includes audio, and it needs a few seconds of replay to show.

diag-written-rate.short: How fast the recording file is growing.
diag-written-rate.eli5: This is the real amount of video and audio written to your file over the last few seconds, not the quality you picked. It shows a dash when you are not recording.

diag-writer-backlog.short: Data waiting to be saved to disk.
diag-writer-backlog.eli5: Recorded data waits here until your drive writes it. A small number is normal. If it climbs toward the limit, your drive is too slow and the recording will stop to keep what it has.

diag-encoded-frames.short: Pictures sent to the video encoder.
diag-encoded-frames.eli5: Every frame Backsight compresses counts here. It just keeps going up while Instant Replay runs.

diag-encoder-queue.eli5: Some frames wait inside the encoder before they come out. A small steady number is normal. A number that keeps growing means your encoder can't keep up.

diag-dropped-frames.short: Frames thrown away because the game was faster.
diag-dropped-frames.eli5: If your game draws more frames than you record, Backsight keeps the newest and drops the rest. That is normal and not a problem.

diag-repeated-frames.short: Frames shown twice because nothing new arrived.
diag-repeated-frames.eli5: When the screen doesn't change, or capture is late, Backsight repeats the last picture to keep the video smooth. Lots of repeats can mean the game is slower than your recording rate.

diag-skipped-frames.short: Frames left out after a long freeze.
diag-skipped-frames.eli5: After a long stall, Backsight jumps ahead instead of sending a burst of repeats. A few after a PC sleep are normal.

diag-late-frames.short: Frames encoded more than one frame late.
diag-late-frames.eli5: A frame is late when the GPU or encoder took too long to handle it. A few are fine. Many mean your PC is too busy, so try a lighter video setting.

diag-silence-fills.short: Quiet gaps added to keep sound in step.
diag-silence-fills.eli5: When nothing is playing, or a device changes, Backsight adds silence so the sound stays in step with the video. Lots of fills while sound is playing means something is wrong.

diag-audio-trimmed.short: Overlapping sound that was cut away.
diag-audio-trimmed.eli5: Sometimes a device sends sound that overlaps what is already saved. Backsight cuts the extra so nothing plays twice.

diag-audio-jumps.eli5: After your PC sleeps or freezes, Backsight skips ahead in the audio instead of filling the gap with silence.

diag-audio-glitches.short: Hiccups reported by your sound device.
diag-audio-glitches.eli5: Windows sometimes tells Backsight that a sound packet came out glitchy. A few over a long session are normal.

diag-audio-device-errors.short: Times a sound device failed or vanished.
diag-audio-device-errors.eli5: This counts unplugged headsets, devices that wouldn't open, and restarts of the Windows audio service. Backsight retries every half second.
